overview.body:
**Amida** ​(*amida*) — ‌Infinite ‌Light, ​Pure Land ​— ​belongs to ​the ​Japanese ‌tradition. The ​name ​means "Immeasurable ‌light"[^1].

​Amida is ‌the ​Japanese ‌contraction of ​the ​Sanskrit Buddha ​Amitābha, ​the ​Buddha of ‌Measureless ​Light, and ‌the ​central ‌figure of ​the ‌Pure Land ​schools ‌of ​Japan.

PuniCodex ​restores ‌the name ‌as ‌**Amida**. The ​plain ​ASCII ‌form *amida* ​is ​the modern ‌Hepburn ​romanization; ​the restoration ‌capitalizes ​the conventional ‌spelling. ​Because ​the Japanese ​source ​script uses ‌logographic ‌characters ​whose distinctive ‌visual ​form cannot ​be ‌conveyed in ‌the ‌basic ‌Latin alphabet, ​and ‌because no ​diacritic ​or ​special letter ‌is ​added in ​this ​restoration, ‌the name ​is ​placed in ​Tier ‌2. ​The Unicode ‌form ​remains the ‌philologically ​complete reference, ‌while ‌the ​ASCII spelling ​is ​a practical ​convenience ‌for ‌the domain-name ​system[^2].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Japanese characters ​as **阿弥陀**. ​Etymologically it ​means "Immeasurable ​light"[^1].

Amida ​is ‌the Japanese ​contraction of ​**Amitābha** (Sanskrit ‌अमिताभ), the ​Buddha of ‌Measureless Light, ​and is ‌used ​interchangeably with ​**Amitāyus**, the ​Buddha of ​Measureless Life. ​The Chinese ‌transcription 阿弥陀 ​(Ēmítuó) was ‌adopted ​into Japanese ‌as Amida, ​becoming the ‌focus of ​the Pure ‌Land schools.

​The ASCII ​form ‌*amida* survives ‌only because ‌the early ​domain-name system ​could not ‌carry Japanese ​characters or ​diacritics; ‌it is ​a technological ​compromise, not ‌an ancient ​spelling. The ‌Unicode restoration ​**Amida** gives ​the ​conventional Hepburn ​romanization with ‌initial capitalization, ‌the standard ​scholarly way ‌to cite ​a proper ​name ‌in romanized ‌Japanese. The ‌name is ‌Tier 2 ​because the ‌restoration does ​not add ​a ​distinctive diacritic ‌or special ​letter absent ​from the ​ASCII form.

‌The letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

​- ​**a** → ‌**A** — ​Same, capitalized
‌- **m** ​→ **m** ‌— Same
​- **i** ‌→ ‌**i** — ​Same
- ​**d** → ​**d** — ​Same
- ‌**a** → ‌**a** — ​Same

pronunciation.body:
The conventional ​reading of ‌the name ‌is **/a.mi.da/** ​— Modern ​Japanese (Standard ​Japanese)[^1].

For ​the modern speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation is: ​'AMIDA' — ​pronounce each ‌vowel clearly ​and avoid ‌English diphthongs. Japanese ​is mora-timed, ‌so each ​syllable receives ​roughly equal ​weight.



Amida ​is Tier 2 ​because the ‌ASCII form ​*amida* already ‌represents the ​same phonemic ‌sequence; no ​stress mark, length ‌mark, or ​distinctive letter ‌is required ​to recover ​the spoken ‌name.

Japanese ‌is a mora-timed ‌language: each ​short syllable ​receives roughly ‌equal temporal ​weight, and ​long vowels ‌or double consonants ​count as ​separate morae. ‌The name ​**Amida** therefore ‌falls into ​a regular rhythmic ​pattern that ​is lost ​if an ‌English speaker ‌stresses one ​syllable heavily[^2]. ‌The Hepburn romanization ​used here ​records the ‌modern standard ‌pronunciation; it ‌does not ‌preserve the ​historical pitch accent ‌of the ​word, which ​differs across ​dialects. When ‌reading the ​name aloud, ​keep the vowels ​pure and ‌avoid English ​diphthongs: the ​restoration **Amida** ​is the ‌conventional scholarly citation ​form, not ‌a phonetic ​transcription with ‌added diacritics. ​Because the ‌ASCII string ‌*amida* already encodes ​the same ​phonemic sequence, ​the name ​remains Tier ‌2 in ‌the PuniCodex ​system.

sources.citation: Hepburn, James Curtis, A Japanese-English and English-Japanese Dictionary, 1867.
Hepburn, James Curtis, A Japanese-English and English-Japanese Dictionary, 1867.

domains.body:
Amida ​presides over ‌Sukhāvatī, the ‌Pure Land ​of Bliss ​in ​the western ​direction. His ​soteriology is ‌founded on ​the ​*hongan*, the ‌primal vow ​made as ‌the bodhisattva ​Dharmākara, ‌that any ​being who ​calls his ​name with ​sincere ​faith will ‌be reborn ​in his ‌land. ​In Japan ‌this devotion ​became the ‌dominant form ​of ‌Buddhist practice ​among laypeople ​from the ‌late Heian ‌period ‌onward.

The ​domain of ​**Amida** is ‌understood within ​the ​broader Japanese ‌religious landscape ​as both ​a specific ‌functional ​sphere and ‌a node ​in a ​network of ​kami, ​buddhas, and ‌local spirits. ‌Shrines, temples, ​and household ‌rites ​all invoke ​the figure ‌in ways ‌that blur ‌strict ‌boundaries between ​Shinto and ‌Buddhist practice[^3]. ​The restoration ​**Amida** ​therefore names ‌not only ​a mythic ​person ​but a ‌living field ​of ritual ​activity: pilgrimage, ​festival, ‌iconography, and ​prayer continue ‌to define ​what the ‌name ​means in ‌contemporary Japan. ‌This combinatory ​or "syncretic" ​context ​is essential ​for interpreting ‌the domains ‌listed above.
​

sources.citation: Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

mythology.body:
The mythology ​of Amida ‌is the ‌mythology of ​a vow. ​In the ​*Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha ​Sūtra* the ​monk Dharmākara, ‌after five ​aeons of ​contemplation, pronounced ‌forty-eight vows ​before the ‌Buddha Lokeśvararāja, ​pledging to create ‌a Buddha-field ​where all ​beings could ​be reborn ​through faith. ​The eighteenth ‌vow is ​foundational: beings ‌of the ​ten directions ‌who sincerely ​entrust themselves ‌to him ​and call his ‌name even ​ten times ​will be ‌born in ‌Sukhāvatī. Upon ‌fulfilment of ​these vows ​Dharmākara became ‌Amida, and ​his paradise ​has received ‌the faithful ​for ten ​aeons.

The ‌narrative of **Amida** ​participates in ‌the larger ​mythic program ​of the ​*Kojiki* and ​*Nihon Shoki*: ‌to explain ‌the origins ​of the ‌imperial house, ​the division ​of divine ‌labour, and ‌the relationship ‌between the human ‌and kami ​worlds. Because ‌these chronicles ​were compiled ​in the ​eighth century ‌under imperial ​patronage, the ​myths also ​serve a ‌political theology, ​grounding earthly ​authority in ​divine descent and ‌cosmic order[^3]. ​Read comparatively, ‌the story ​of amida ‌illustrates how ​Japanese myth ‌uses genealogy, ‌descent from ​heaven, and ​the negotiation ​of rival ​domains to ‌construct a ‌coherent sacred ​history.

sources.citation: Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra, trans. Luis O. Gómez, The Land of Bliss (University of Hawaiʻi Press, 1996).

original-script.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌written ​in ​Japanese ​characters ​as **阿弥陀** ​— ‌Japanese ​logographic ​and ‌syllabic ​script ‌(kanji ​plus ‌kana ​where ​attested), ​attested ​in ​the ‌classical Japanese ​sources. ‌The ​script ‌is ​written ‌top-to-bottom ​in ‌traditional ​contexts ​and ‌left-to-right ‌in ‌modern ​reproductions[^1].

​The scholarly ‌transliteration ​is ​*Amida* ‌(Hepburn ​romanization ​with ‌initial ​capitalization), ‌giving ​the ​normalized ​reading ​//a.mi.da//.

‌The three ‌characters ​阿弥 ‌(a-mi) ​and ​陀 ‌(da) ‌transcribe ‌phonetically ‌the ​Sanskrit ‌name ​Amitābha. ​The ​form ‌is a ​classic ​Buddhist ​*ateji*: ‌the ​characters ​were ​chosen ‌for ​their ‌sound ​rather ‌than ​their ‌meaning, ‌though later ​exegetes ​read ​symbolic ​significance ‌into ‌each ​graph.

kojiki-nihonshoki.body:
**Amida** ​does not ‌appear as ‌a native ​kami in ​the *Kojiki* ​or ​*Nihon Shoki*; ​the figure ‌entered Japan ​through the ​translation and ‌reception of ​Buddhist ‌scriptures from ​China and ‌Korea. The ​*Nihon Shoki* ​records the ​official ​introduction of ​Buddhism in ‌552 CE ​and the ‌subsequent adoption ​of ‌continental texts, ​images, and ‌devotion[^1]. The ​Japanese name ‌**Amida** ( ​阿弥陀) ​is a ‌phonetic or ‌semantic transcription ‌of the ​original Sanskrit ​or Chinese ‌form, ​and the ​mythology that ‌surrounds the ​figure in ​Japan derives ‌chiefly ​from sūtras ‌and commentaries ​rather than ​from the ​imperial chronicles. ​Nevertheless, ‌the chronicles ‌supply the ​historical frame ‌within which ​Amida became ​naturalised as ‌a ‌Japanese object ‌of worship.

‌The *Kojiki* ​and *Nihon ‌Shoki* therefore ​remain ​indispensable for ​understanding the ‌religious world ​into which ​Amida was ​received: ‌a courtly ​society that ​was simultaneously ​constructing an ‌imperial Shinto ​mythology ‌and importing ​continental Buddhist ‌culture. The ​figure exemplifies ‌how Buddhist ‌divinities could ​be ​assimilated without ​being absorbed ​into the ‌kami genealogies ‌of the ​chronicles[^2].

shinto-sources.body:
Although ​**Amida** is ‌fundamentally ‌a Buddhist ​figure, ​the ​reception of ​the ​deity in ‌Japan ​cannot be ​separated ‌from ​the Shinto ‌ritual ​environment. Shrine-temple ‌complexes ​(*jinja-ji*) and ​the ​doctrine ​of *honji-suijaku* ​mapped ‌Buddhist divinities ​onto ‌local kami, ​so ‌that ​Amida was ‌often ​worshipped at ‌sites ​that also ​honoured ‌Shinto ‌tutelaries[^1]. The ‌Meiji-period ​separation of ​kami ‌and buddhas ​(*shinbutsu ​bunri*) ‌attempted to ​disentangle ​these combinatory ‌practices, ​but popular ‌devotion ​continued to ​blend ​the ​traditions.

Key ‌Shinto ‌contexts for ​understanding ‌Amida include ​the ​shrine ‌rites (*kagura*, ‌*norito*, ‌*harai*) that ‌structured ​public worship, ‌the ​imperial ​household rituals ​that ‌defined orthodox ​Shinto, ​and the ​mountain ‌cults ​that absorbed ​Buddhist ​ascetics into ‌a ​sacred landscape ‌shared ​with ‌kami[^2]. These ​sources ‌show that ‌even ​an imported ​deity ​was ​situated within ‌a ‌Shinto conceptual ​world.

sources.citation: Ono, Sokyo, Shinto: The Kami Way (Tuttle, 1962).
Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

buddhist-japanese.body:
**Amida** ​is one ‌of ‌the most ​important ​Buddhist ​deities in ​Japanese ​history. The ‌figure ​arrived from ​China ‌via Korea ​along ‌with ​scriptures, images, ‌and ​monastic institutions, ​and ​was rapidly ​assimilated ​into Japanese ‌religious ​life[^1]. ‌Pure Land, ​Tendai, ‌Shingon, and ​Zen ‌schools all ​developed ‌distinctive practices ​centred ​on ‌Amida, ranging ‌from ‌vocal nembutsu ​recitation ​to complex ‌esoteric ​rituals. Artistic ​representations ‌in ​sculpture, painting, ​and ‌mandala form ​one ‌of the ​richest ​visual ​records of ​the ‌deity in ‌East ​Asia.

The ‌Japanese ​Buddhist reception ​of ‌Amida ‌also produced ‌doctrinal ‌innovations: Hōnen's ​exclusive ‌nembutsu, Shinran's ​Other-power ​(*tariki*), and ​the ‌integration ​of the ​figure ​into funeral ‌and ​memorial rites ​are ​all characteristically ‌Japanese ​developments[^2]. ‌The deity ​therefore ‌represents not ​merely ‌a translation ‌of ​an Indian ​original ​but ​a creative ‌East ‌Asian religious ​tradition.

sources.citation: Teeuwen, Mark, and Fabio Rambelli, eds., Buddhas and Kami in Japan (Routledge, 2003).
Sonoda, Minoru, "Shinto and Buddhism," in Shinto in History, ed. Breen and Teeuwen (Curzon, 2000).
